habitat: Spotted bats inhabit arid and semi-arid regions of western North America, from British Columbia through the western United States to northern Mexico. They are found in deserts, grasslands, open coniferous forests, and canyonlands — often in rugged, rocky terrain. During the day, they roost in cliff-face crevices, rock fissures, and occasionally buildings. They are one of the few bat species that roosts almost exclusively in rock crevices on vertical cliff faces, making them challenging to study.
diet: Spotted bats are insectivorous specialists, feeding almost exclusively on moths — particularly owlet moths and other large Lepidoptera. They are 'aerial hawkers,' catching flying insects in open air using echolocation. Their echolocation calls are among the lowest frequency of any bat (9-12 kHz), and unlike most bats, their calls are partially audible to humans as faint, high-pitched clicks. The low frequency carries well in open terrain, helping them detect moths at longer ranges.
behavior: Spotted bats are solitary and emerge late in the evening, well after dark — one of the latest-emerging bat species. They fly high (10-30 meters above ground) and fast in open terrain. They are highly mobile and may travel long distances between roosts and foraging areas. Females give birth to a single pup. Unlike many bats, they do not form large maternity colonies. Their roosts on cliff faces provide exceptional protection from predators, but make them difficult to locate and study.
facts: The spotted bat is one of North America's most beautiful and distinctive bat species, with three prominent white spots on its otherwise jet-black back and enormous pink ears — among the largest in proportion to body size of any North American mammal. Their ears can measure over 40 mm. Their echolocation is loudest at 9-12 kHz, a frequency so low that it overlaps with the hearing range of some humans — making them one of the few 'audible' bats. They are considered one of the least-studied bat species due to their cliff-roosting habits and remote habitats.
naming: Spotted bat names might reflect their three white spots, enormous pink ears, or audible echolocation. Consider names like Spot, Domino, Radar, Echo, Pinky, Speckle, Phantom, Patches, Cliff, Flare (for their large ears), or Vesper.
